div.p: Online energy-efficient real-time task scheduling for a heterogeneous multicore system is complicated because of the synergistic processing between cores and trade-off between energy conservation and schedulability. This paper proposes a multicore energy efficiency ratio for minimizing energy consumption and a bandwidth reservation algorithm for improving quality of service for applications. The performance of the proposed methodology was evaluated using a series of workloads, and encouraging results were obtained.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Most modern multimedia handheld devices contain a heterogeneous multicore system-on-a-chip, which generally contains multiple general purpose processor (GPP) and special purpose processor (SPP) cores [1], such as Nvdia Tegra 4 and AMD APU, for realizing optimal performance and energy efficiency. Therefore, minimizing energy consumption in such systems is a major concern. Contrary to homogeneous multicore systems, GPP and SPP cores have different properties; the SPP core, for example, demonstrates rapid execution and substantial context switch overhead. To ensure quality of service for applications in such systems, the applications are implemented as distinct functions, which might be executed in a specific cores. However, energy-efficient real-time task scheduling in a heterogeneous multicore system-on-a-chip is complex because of the precedence constraints of the functions and trade-off between energy conservation and schedulability.

Numerous studies have investigated energy-aware real-time scheduling in heterogeneous multicore systems [2,3,4,5]. Some studies [2,3] have focused on systems with the same instruction set architecture (ISA), for example, ARM big.LITTLE architecture. [2] proposed workload-based task assignment, and [3] proposed approximation-aware scheduling that determines a near-optimal schedule and frequency assignment in the offline mode and improves the quality of service and energy conservation at runtime. However, these studies have focused on energy-efficient task scheduling for single-ISA multicore systems, which involve tasks without precedence constraints. Regarding heterogeneous ISA, [4] implemented a machine-learning algorithm in context-aware applications for reducing energy consumption and improving performance, and [5] used mixed integer linear programming for statically assigning a task execution frequency. However, these studies have focused on offline optimization scheduling without accounting for runtime dynamic workloads.

For addressing runtime and precedence constraint task scheduling problems on heterogeneous multicore systems with heterogeneous ISA, [6,7] proposed scheduling frameworks for resolving the precedence constraints of tasks. Moreover, [8] presented a graphical processing unit (GPU) scheduler, which is asynchronous and non-preemptive, for managing GPU resources. By considering energy minimization, some studies [9,10] have adopted non-preemptive SPP cores, which switch the power status for devices and the voltage scaling for processors, as resources. However, the considerable blocking time of SPP cores may dramatically increase energy consumption and reduce system applicability. [11] proposed an energy efficiency ratio (EER) based on the scheduling framework proposed by [6] for a heterogeneous dual-core system. The dual-core system comprises GPP and SPP cores. In the absence of partition imbalance on such a system, the main idea of the EER is to assign a lower execution frequency to the core with a high power consumption. However, in a heterogeneous multicore system, the partition-based scheduler might unbalance the workload, which causes redundant energy consumption and system utilization degradation. Similar to the difference in uniprocessor and multiprocessor scheduling, an unbalanced workload among cores makes the trade-off between energy efficiency and system utilization more complicated. This study not only presents a multicore energy efficiency ratio (MEER) to trade-off power consumption among cores with varied power characteristics but also proposes a bandwidth reservation to improve the workload balance among cores with the same power characteristics for increasing system schedulability.

To realize online energy-efficient real-time task scheduling for heterogeneous multicore systems, three essential technical problems must be addressed: 1) What frequency should be assigned to cores with varied power characteristics for minimizing energy consumption? 2) What bandwidth should be assigned to tasks with a precedence constraint for satisfying timing constraints? 3) How to trade-off energy conservation and schedulability considering SPP properties, such as semipartition execution?

In contrast to offline optimization approaches, this study was motivated by a desire to investigate the complexities introduced by the trade-off between energy efficiency and system utilization for heterogeneous multicore systems. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• An online energy-efficient task scheduling framework was proposed for dynamically managing energy consumption and ensuring quality of service for applications in heterogeneous multicore systems. • A method was proposed for determining the MEER to minimize energy consumption by considering the hardware properties of the system architecture and execution dependency between heterogeneous cores. • A methodology was presented for reserving the bandwidths of tasks among multicore systems to trade-off energy consumption and schedulability.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: This study addressed the energy-efficient real-time scheduling of periodic tasks in a heterogeneous multicore system. We assumed that the system comprises multiple GPP and SPP cores. Given a set of GPP cores G = {G 1 , G 2 , . . . , G m } and a set of SPP cores S = {S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S n }, the power consumption for GPP and SPP is denoted as P G and P S , respectively. The power consumption functions of each core can be modeled as resultant dynamic power consumption, caused by the switching activity in a circuit, and leakage power consumption, which is present even when no logic operations are performed [12]. The dynamic power consumption is related to the core's operating frequency f and can be modeled as

div.p: To ensure quality of service, most applications set timing and precedence constraints in a heterogeneous multicore system. Applications are executed by the GPP first, which subsequently binds one available SPP through a mailbox to accelerate the special purpose functions. The SPP cores then execute their functions asynchronously with the GPP for multicore data parallelism and then copy the results back to the GPP through shared memory. In this study, we assumed that given a set of applications (tasks) T = T G T S = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ h }, each application is characterized by a tuple {c p ,d p }, where c p is the worst-case execution cycle, and d p is the relative deadline for task τ p , which was assumed to be equal to the task period. The relative deadline is the maximum allowable response time of each instant of a periodic task. The response time is the duration from the instant of task arrival to the instant of task completion. Task utilization u p is the ratio of the worst-case execution time estimated using the maximum execution frequency to its relative deadline. Task τ p comprises a set of subtasks τ p,q that enables the completion of multiple functions. The subtasks of a given task are alternately processed through the GPP and SPP. In practice, at the system design stage, each function is implemented as a GPP or SPP function. In the present study, we assumed that all subtasks are statically assigned to the GPP or SPP, and focused on scheduling problems

As shown in Fig. 1, when subtask τ p,q is executed by the GPP, subtask τ p,q+1 is executed by the SPP. The subtasks executed by the GPP and SPP are called GPP and SPP subtasks, respectively. T G and T S are task subsets of the subtasks of all tasks executed by GPP and SPP, respectively; i.e., for task τ p , subtasks {τ p,1 , τ p,3 , . . . τ p,̟ } ∈ T G and subtasks {τ p,2 , τ p,4 , . . . τ p,̟-1 } ∈ T S . The total worst-case execution cycles of the GPP and SPP subtasks of a task τ p are denoted as c G p and c S p , respectively. In the shared memory model, the worst-case communication time can be bounded or analyzed as a part of the worst-case execution time. The implementation of the communication and coexecution architecture was discussed in [14]. In this study, the execution time included the communication cost without special identification. The SPP is typically non-preemptive to avoid a substan-tial context switch overhead (η); however, non-preemptive scheduling may degrade the schedulability of the applications because of a large number of blocking cycles. An SPP proposed in a recent study [8] provides a specific command for semi-preemptive tasks that can be interrupted within a specific period; therefore, a high-priority application can preempt a low-priority application. In this study, task scheduling in the GPP was preemptive, whereas task execution in the SPP was semi-preemptive. As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), applications τ 1 and τ 2 arrive at times a 1 and a 2 , respectively. The deadline D 1 for τ 1 is after deadline D 2 for τ 2 . Subtask τ 2,2 of task τ 2 can be executed in the SPP when subtask τ 2,1 is completed in the GPP. However, subtask τ 1,2 of task τ 1 is executed in the SPP at that time; therefore, τ 2,2 is blocked until the preemption point is reached, following which τ 2,2 preempts τ 1,2 , and twice the number of context switches (2η) are performed. For the same example, when non-preemptive scheduling is applied in the SPP, τ 2,2 is blocked until τ 1,2 is completed and then violates the deadline (Fig. 2(b)). The blocking cycles from the semi-preemptive scheduling technique are bounded by the maximum length of the preemption point interval (ρ); this provides a more favorable schedulability of the applications compared with non-preemptive scheduling.

Problem definition Consider a system comprising sets of GPP cores G = {G 1 , G 2 , . . . , G m } and SPP cores S = {S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S n } as well as a set of tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ h } such that each task comprises a set of subtasks with precedence constraints, and each subtask is statically assigned as a GPP or SPP subtask. Through task partition, subtask τ p,q assigned to the GPP core G i or SPP core S j is defined as τ p,q ∈ T Gi or τ p,q ∈ T Sj , respectively. Furthermore, each GPP core G i and SPP core S j are associated with a common power consumption function

div.head: III. ENERGY-EFFICIENT TASK SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK
div.p: FOR HETEROGENEOUS MULTICORE SYSTEMS This section presents the concept and mechanisms of the proposed energy-efficient task scheduling framework, referred to as energy-efficient heterogeneous multicore scheduling (EHMS), for heterogeneous multicore systems. Section III-A introduces the online scheduling framework. Section III-B proposes a concept, MEER, for addressing the frequency precedence between cores to minimize the energy consumption. Section III-C presents a bandwidth reservation (frequency assignment) algorithm for compromising schedulability and energy conservation. Section III-D introduces an admission control for ensuring the schedulability of tasks.

div.head: A. Framework
div.p: We explored the energy-efficient heterogeneous multicore real-time task scheduling problem and proposed a framework (Fig. 3). To account for the precedence constraints of tasks and semi-preemption property of SPP cores, a bandwidth reservation scheduling framework was proposed in [6]. We extended the scheduling framework in [6] with energy efficiency considerations for a heterogeneous multicore system. During runtime, each new task is scheduled through a partitionbased dispatcher. For saving energy without deadline violation, the MEER is estimated according to the current system workload and hardware properties. To trade-off schedulability and energy saving in the multicore system, a bandwidth is then assigned to each task on the basis of the MEER and the total utilization of tasks. Each bandwidth server with an assigned bandwidth (server size) is dispatched into GPP and SPP cores through the Worst-Fit-Decreasing (WFD) dispatcher for improving the ability of energy saving2 . All tasks are then scheduled through the assigned bandwidth by using a dedicated bandwidth server and a deadline-driven scheduler at each core, and are executed at the minimum required frequency on the basis of the total required bandwidth of each core.

div.head: B. Multicore Energy Efficiency Ratio
div.p: In contrast to a homogeneous multicore system, in a heterogeneous multicore system, the GPP and SPP demonstrate a master-slave relationship. Lower execution frequencies on GPP cores may increase the required frequencies of SPP cores to meet the end-to-end deadlines of tasks. In addition to the schedulability problem, the power characteristics of the SPP may differ from those of the GPP, and this may Fig. 3: The energy-efficient heterogeneous multicore scheduling framework result in different energy consumptions at the same execution frequency. For resolving the frequency dependency problems in such systems, the concept of the EER for a heterogeneous dual-core system, which comprised GPP and SPP cores, was presented in [11]. The main objective of [11] was to assign a low execution frequency to cores with a high power consumption. Unlike heterogeneous dual-core systems, unbalanced workloads among cores might cause considerable blocking time for a task in a heterogeneous multicore system. In other words, unbalanced workloads among cores make the trade-off between energy efficiency and system utilization more complicated. For example, a lower execution frequency of cores increases the absolute execution time of subtasks, resulting in a more unbalanced workload among cores. Increasing the execution frequency to balance the workload can result in more tasks meeting the timing constraint; however, it increases the energy consumption, particularly for the core with higher power characteristics. To minimize the energy consumption under timing constraints in heterogeneous multicore systems, an approach to determine the MEER is proposed in this paper (Algorithm 1).

An ideal frequency ratio (MEER) between the GPP and the SPP cores is determined for resolving the frequency dependency between the GPP and SPP cores by assuming that the workloads among the homogenous cores are balanced and by considering the varied power characteristics of the cores. Subsequently, the bandwidth reservation scheme is proposed in Section III-C to improve the schedulability by considering unbalanced workloads.

To address the precedence constraints scheduling of subtasks according to the concept proposed in [6], all tasks are scheduled through bandwidth servers during runtime. When the bandwidth server is applied to the system, each subtask can be considered an independent sporadic job and scheduled according to the deadline, i.e., Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF). A technical problem is the partition of an end-to-end deadline of the GPP and SPP subtasks to meet the timing constraints. We applied the proportional deadline partition [16] with core utilization to manage the effect of schedulability and minimize the energy consumption. As shown in Algorithm 1, the total

To minimize the energy consumption of the system E system , based on the extreme value theorem, the value of MEER can be determined when dE system dMEER = 0. Several methods, e.g., bisection and Newton's method, exist for determining the MEER (Step 6). div.head: Fig. 4: Precedence constraint resolution
div.p: According to the optimal solution proposed in [17], each task can meet the timing constraints when the assigned frequency is no less than that required for utilization. In a heterogeneous multicore system, each task is first scheduled for the GPP, and each SPP subtask is issued by a GPP subtask. This task is suspended in the GPP when it is being executed in the SPP and is resumed when the execution in the SPP is completed. As shown in Fig. 4, bounding the response time of each SPP subtask separates any two GPP subtasks, and the duration of each separation is bounded by the given local relative deadline, i.e., D p,q -a p,q . With this assumption, GPP and SPP subtasks of a task can be considered a set of sporadic jobs, and all GPP and SPP subtasks of the corresponding task can be scheduled through dedicated GPP and SPP bandwidth servers, respectively. To meet the end-to-end deadline of each task (e.g., D p for task τ p in Fig. 4), the technique question is how much bandwidth shall be reserved for each server such that the total response time (the deadlines assigned by the server) of all subtasks of the task is no more than the deadline. The concept of using bandwidth servers to execute subtasks on heterogeneous multicore systems was proposed in [6]; this study continued the investigation of heterogeneous multicore systems. The frequency assignment problem was thus transformed into a bandwidth reservation problem, and the bandwidth of each task was determined for scheduling the corresponding subtasks on GPP and SPP cores.

The objective is to assign bandwidths for GPP and SPP subtasks on the basis of the MEER for energy minimization under the timing constraint. When the workload is high, to improve schedulability, the bandwidth of each task is adjusted such that the total required bandwidth of all cores of the same type is no more than the schedulability bound for the given scheduler and dispatcher. In this study, the total bandwidth server (TBS) and the EDF with the partition-based WFD dispatcher [15] were applied to achieve improved timeliness and energy saving.

Generally, the number of GPP cores is less than the number of SPP cores. After assigning a bandwidth to each task, scheduling GPP (SPP) subtasks of each task can be considered an independent task. The task dispatch is transformed into the server dispatch. Through the WFD dispatcher, all the servers are sorted by the appropriate GPP and SPP bandwidths in the decreasing order (Steps 25 and 34), and each server is assigned to the core with the minimum bandwidth (Steps 26-28 and 35-37). To satisfy the timing constraints, the total required bandwidth of each core must be less than 1 [15] (Steps 29-31 and 38-40). If the summation of the required bandwidths of GPP (SPP) subtasks of task τ p and the total bandwidth of a core (G µ or S ν ) exceeds 1, task τ p is not schedulable and is dropped (Steps 33 and 42). Task τ p might be schedulable during runtime. However, to manage the new arrival tasks and provide system robustness, a sufficient admission control with low complexity is applied. Execution frequencies for GPP and SPP cores are assigned (Steps 43-46) according to the corresponding total bandwidth. At runtime, each GPP and SPP core executes all the subtasks on the assigned frequency without dynamic scaling.

After frequency assignment, all tasks are scheduled through the corresponding server according to the EHMS framework, as shown in Fig. 3, during runtime. The time complexity of Bandwidth Reservation is O(h(m + n)), where h is the number of tasks, and m and n are the number of GPP and SPP cores, respectively. The Bandwidth Reservation can be invoked during runtime to manage the new arrival tasks because of the low time complexity.

Any two GPP (SPP) subtasks of a task do not overlap because of the precedence constraint; therefore, there is only one GPP (SPP) subtask of each task being scheduled in a GPP (SPP) at any time. Hence, the GPP (SPP) utilization of a task is less than the maximum GPP (SPP) utilization of any subtask of this task and is bounded by the bandwidth of this task. div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: We compared our approach EHMS with the related works [11,22] by conducting experiments entailing the use of different system architectures and workloads. Section IV-A presents the experimental settings. Sections IV-B1 and IV-B2 present the energy consumption results obtained by evaluating task sets with different total utilizations for varied number of GPP cores and varied power characteristics of the SPP cores, respectively. 4 When the core is executed at a frequency lower than the maximum frequency, the response time of each task τp is ∀τp,q ∈T G i cp,q f G i + ∀τp,q ∈T S j 2η+cp,q +ρ f S j ≤ dp. By using Eqs. 16 and 17, the values of λ G p and λ S p are no larger than f G i and f S j , respectively. Therefore, Eq. 15 is used in the sufficient schedulability test. 5(a) and 6, the energy consumption for EHDS-R, EMap, and EHMS is decreased because the higher power property γ S increases from 2 to 3 and provides higher energy saving ability. When the utilization is low (i.e., less than 3), the lower execution frequency can considerably reduce the energy consumption caused by dynamic power consumption. However, the excessively low frequency may cause a bottleneck during energy saving because most of the energy is consumed by the leakage power. Therefore, the performance gap between the EHMS and the EHDS-R narrows as task utilization decreases when the higher power property of the SPP is considered. In contrast to EHMS and EHDS-R, EMap employs the first-fit algorithm; the assigned frequencies are relatively higher than those in EHMS and EHDS-R; therefore, the energy saving is not bounded by the leakage power consumption. Compared with EHDS-R and EMap, the energy saving of the proposed EHMS is higher by 22.4% and 35.6%, respectively.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: This study explored online energy-efficient real-time task scheduling for heterogeneous multicore systems. The MEER concept and bandwidth reservation algorithm are proposed for providing optimal schedulability and energy efficiency. In the proposed MEER, the power characteristics of the system architecture and current workload are considered for minimizing energy consumption. The bandwidth reservation algorithm maximizes the schedulability with considering precedence constraints and multicore task scheduling. Runtime frequency scaling of each core depends on the total required bandwidth. The performance levels of the proposed system were evaluated using a series of experiments, and encouraging results indicating minimized energy consumption and schedulability were obtained. We intend to explore online thermal-aware real-time scheduling for such systems in the future.

div.head: A. Experimental Setting
div.p: In this section, we compare the energy consumption of the proposed EHMS with that of the revised EHDS (EHDS-R) [11] and EMap [22]. In EHMS and EHDS-R, each task with a precedence constraint is scheduled through the bandwidth server with EDF scheduling. Because EHDS is proposed for heterogeneous dual-core systems, which only comprise a GPP and SPP core, EHDS is revised as EHDS-R for multicore heterogeneous systems as follows. If the EER for EHDS [11] is 3 √ 2 and the ratio of the number of GPP cores to the number of SPP cores is m n , then the EER in the EHDS-R is revised as 3 √ 2 m n . All tasks are dispatched through the WFD dispatcher for both EHMS and EHDS-R. Moreover, for EHMS, all evaluated task sets passed the schedulability test (Theorem 3.5) without runtime deadline violation. For EMap, all tasks are scheduled through EDF and dispatched using first fit. After invoking task partition, the core frequency is assigned as the maximum value of the ratio of the corresponding core utilization and maximum density of the given task deadline. The density is the ratio of the summation of the execution time of all tasks with a deadline shorter than the deadline of the current task to the considered deadline. In the experiments, a system-on-a-chip comprising 4 GPP cores and 16 SPP cores was used for evaluation; the power consumption was assumed to be P G (f Gi ) = (0.45f 3 Gi + 0.04) W for the GPP and P S (f Sj ) = (0.9f 2 Sj + 0.04) W for the SPP. All tasks were executed using any frequency in the given range, in which the maximum and minimum available frequencies were normalized to 1 and 0.1, respectively, and the frequencies were rounded off to the second decimal place. The context switch time η and interval between the two preemption points ρ were set to half of the maximum execution cycles of the SPP subtasks, i.e., 0.5 max τp,q∈TS {c p,q }. The energy consumption of each context switch was set to P S (f max S ) × 0.5 max τp,q∈TS {c p,q }. The workloads in the experiments were generated randomly. The total task utilization of the system ranged from 1 to 7. The generated periods of each task from 110250 to 220500 cycles. The ratio of the total GPP subtask utilization to the total SPP subtask utilization was set to 0.4 : 0.6. Each task has 7 subtasks and each subtask was alternately executed at the GPP and SPP cores. Each setting included 50 task sets and each task set contains 60 tasks that were generated to average the experimental results.

The normalized energy consumption was the primary metric. Let X and Y denote the amounts of energy consumed by the evaluated approaches and the EHMS algorithm without dynamic voltage scaling, respectively. The normalized energy consumption of the evaluated algorithm is defined as X/Y .

div.head: B. Experimental Result 1) Varied Number of GPP Cores:
div.p: As shown in Fig. 5(a), the number of GPP and SPP cores are 4 and 16, respectively. The horizontal axis represents the varied task set utilization and the vertical axis represents the normalized energy consumption. The first observation is that the energy consumption of all approaches increases when the task set utilization increases because higher frequencies are assigned to each GPP/SPP core for avoiding timing constraint violation. Comparing EHDS-R and EHMS, the performance gap is narrow when the task set utilization increases from 1 to 3.5. This is because the assigned frequencies for EHDS-R and EHMS are similar when the utilization is low. However, when the task set utilization exceeds 5.0, the given task set is unschedulable for EHDS-R because the bandwidth server reservation of EHDS-R does not consider the utilization bounds of GPP and SPP. This means that the frequency assignment is too low to meet the timing constraint. In contrast to EHDS-R, EHMS increases the frequency of GPP cores to improve the schedulability and reduce the energy consumption of the system. EMap has the lowest system capacity and energy efficiency, because the frequency assignment does not consider the context switch overhead. If the context switch overhead in SPP core is ignorable, the task set with higher total utilization (> 1.5) might be schedulable. In this experiment, we compared the energy consumption without violating the deadline constraint. Finally, the maximal schedulable utilization of EHMS, EHDS-R, and EMap were 6.5, 5.0, and 1.5, respectively. EHMS provides better energy efficiency than EHDS-R and EMap, that is up to 17.7% and 31.3%, respectively.

Comparing Figures 5(a) and 5(b), when the number of GPP cores is decreased from 4 to 2, the energy consumption increases for EHMS, EHDS-R, and EMap. This is because when the number of GPP cores is reduced, the GPP cores increase the execution frequencies for satisfying the timing constraint of GPP subtasks. The performance gap between the EHMS and the EHDS-R increases when the task set utilization increases from 1 to 3.5. Furthermore, EHMS provides superior trade-off between the energy conservation and the schedulability, as shown in Fig. 5(b). EHMS reserves the bandwidth by using the MEER to minimize the energy consumption when the task utilization is low (i.e., < 3.5). When the task utilization is high (i.e., ≥ 3.5), the energy consumption increases because EHMS adjusts the bandwidth without employing the MEER to maximize the schedulability. In contrast to EHMS, EHDS-R determines the EER without considering the workload and only increases the frequency of the SPP cores. As shown in Fig. 5(b), the maximal schedulable utilization of EHMS, EHDS-R, and EMap are 4.0, 3.5, and 1.5, respectively. Compared with EHDS-R and EMap, the energy saving of the proposed EHMS is higher by 20.8% and 27.1%, respectively.
